My new paper, [*Method: Using generalized additive models in the livestock animal sciences*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anopes.2026.100157), is now published in *animal - open space*. It is a practical introduction to GAMs for animal scientists, illustrated with three worked examples: a cow's lactation curve, growth curves for commercial pigs, and an experiment on the effects of maternal thyroid hormones on growth in Japanese quail.

Non-linear relationships are familiar territory in animal science. What is less familiar is allowing the data to inform the shape of those relationships. GAMs extend generalized linear models with smooth functions of covariates. Penalised splines and automatic smoothness selection let us estimate those functions while balancing fit against complexity. The paper starts with a visual explanation of how this works, then moves from models with a single curve to hierarchical models with multiple curves modelling individual animals' responses.

The lactation example is a useful illustration of why the choice of model matters. Here the response is the average daily fat content of milk from a single cow. Wood's lactation model and a Tweedie GLM capture the general rise and fall, but miss the broad peak and a plateau later in lactation. The Tweedie GAM follows these features more closely, and the residuals show much less remaining structure.

![Figure 3 from the paper: fitted lactation curves (a) and response residuals for Wood's model (b), the Tweedie GLM (c), and the Tweedie GAM (d). Bands show 95% uncertainty intervals. Reproduced from Simpson (2026), under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](/assets/img/posts/gams-in-livestock-animal-science-figure-3.png){fig-alt="Lactation curves and residual diagnostics for three models. Panel a compares observed daily milk fat with fitted curves from Wood's model, a Tweedie GLM, and a Tweedie GAM. Panels b to d show patterned residuals for Wood's model and the GLM, and much less structure for the GAM."}

This affects the biological quantities we estimate, too. The GAM places the peak fat content later in lactation and expresses greater uncertainty about its timing, which makes sense for such a broad peak. It also estimates a slower decline midway between the peak and the end of lactation. A model can give a precise answer while missing features of the data that matter to that answer.

The other examples extend this approach to repeated measurements. For the pigs, hierarchical GAMs [@pedersen-miller-etal-2019] estimate an average growth curve together with animal-specific departures from it. For the quail, they allow treatment and sex effects to be assessed while accounting for individual growth curves and maternal effects. The quail analysis finds little evidence of treatment differences in growth rate at day 20 or weight at day 78. These examples show that GAMs can support biological inference as well as describe non-linear patterns.

The paper is [open access](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anopes.2026.100157), and you can also [download the PDF](/assets/reprints/simpson-2026-animal-open-space.pdf). The accompanying [code and data on Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15777270) include R tutorials for fitting the models and reproducing the analyses. If you work with growth curves, lactation data, or other non-linear responses, I hope these examples give you a useful starting point.

On a personal note, this is the first paper I have led since I took the plunge into animal science, working in applied statistics in an animal and veterinary sciences department and joining the tenure track. Previously, my roles had all been in research or consultancy: first at UCL with ENSIS Ltd., the consultancy arm of the Environmental Change Research Centre in UCL Geography, and later with Peter Leavitt at the Institute for Environmental Change and Society (IECS) at the University of Regina in Saskatchewan, Canada. Although I led my own lab at IECS with NSERC funding, I was never on the tenure track. In some ways, moving to Aarhus University was a step back career-wise, and certainly financially. I joined as a Tenure Track Assistant Professor of Applied Statistics (if I remember correctly, the job posting called it *applied biometrics*).

The move from ecology and environmental science to animal science has taken more adjustment than I expected. As a geographer by training who didn't even study biology at A level, I found myself in unfamiliar territory. Much of what I took for granted in ecology has needed rethinking in animal science. Building relationships with new colleagues and finding my own voice and footing have also taken time. Now, nearly five and a half years after joining Aarhus University, with my tenure clock ticking, I finally feel that I am finding my niche here. This paper is the first fruit of that process.
